idiom_name: two hierarchies plus an accept() callback (Element and Visitor) with an explicit traversal policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare one Element interface with a single hook, accept(visitor), and one Visitor interface whose methods are keyed by the concrete element classes. Every concrete element implements accept as a one-line callback into the visitor method for its own class; every concrete visitor implements all methods and owns one operation's state. Decide the traversal policy explicitly — the visitor drives it, the object structure drives it (composite elements recurse into their children from accept), or a separate iterator does — because that choice determines who must change when a new element shape appears. Provide a no-op base visitor so an operation that cares about two node kinds does not have to implement the rest.
pitfalls: Implementing accept() once on the base class with a type test instead of overriding it in each concrete element — the callback then passes the base type and the compiler can no longer check coverage.
Letting every visitor re-implement the traversal: two operations then disagree about visit order and double-visit different nodes.
Skipping the no-op base visitor and growing the Visitor interface without defaults, which breaks every operation at once when a new element is added.
Letting a visitor mutate the structure while it is being walked, unless the traversal policy explicitly supports deferred changes.
